ATLANTA, Georgia  (CNN) -- Stephen Plumlee started feeling dizzy and nauseated shortly after his flight from Sarasota, Florida, landed in Atlanta, Georgia. He was wheeled off the plane by paramedics, but instead of being taken to a hospital emergency room downtown, he was treated in the atrium of the busiest airport in the world. The AeroClinic joins a growing field of easy-access medical facilities found in pharmacies and retail outlets. The AeroClinic, a new retail medical facility, offers quick, inexpensive care to travelers and some of the airport's 55,000 employees. "We're kind of the stop in between the hospital during your travels," said Dr. Dominic Mack, chief medical officer for the clinic. The AeroClinic joins a growing field of easy-access medical facilities found in pharmacies and retail outlets around the country. You could say it falls somewhere between the newer, small clinics and the larger full-service after-hours clinics that have been around for many years. For about $80, a patient can be treated by a doctor or physician assistant for a minor acute illness such as strep throat, upset stomach or headache. That was the reason behind Derrick Gross' visit. The medical sales representative lives in Atlanta, but travels at least three days a week. He says he's too busy to see a regular doctor, and when he saw the sign while passing through the airport, he decided to make an appointment. Gross spent about 20 minutes with physician assistant Sabrina Jackson going through a battery of tests to try to determine the source of his headaches.  Health Minute: Airport clinic gives travelers a health-care alternative ». He received a supply of ibuprofen when the tests revealed no obvious medical problems. "I took a chance by coming here today and I'm satisfied," Gross said. He agreed to follow up with his primary care physician. Mack said he treats a lot of patients like Gross. "You have 250,000 passengers who come through Atlanta Hartsfield every day, and people are sick. What they do is delay their care or they don't get their care at all." Dr. David Satcher, former U.S. surgeon general and frequent flier, sees the need first hand. "I've traveled almost 40,000 miles in the last month and I know there are a lot of people who spend time in airports and a lot of people don't get the care they need," he said. As a member of the American Academy of Family Physicians, Satcher believes the concept of a quick-care health facility inside an airport is a good one so long as patients continue to have contact with a primary care physician at home. He serves on the board of directors for The AeroClinic and is one of the privately held company's original investors. He wants potential patients to understand the restrictions of a facility such as The AeroClinic. "This is not the place to go when you're having chest pains. ... (But) obviously, if you have a minor illness this is an opportunity to seek care while you're traveling and not have to wait until you get back home." The clinic's 12 staffers also offer preventive care including physical exams, routine vaccinations and monitoring of chronic diseases. The facility accepts some insurance coverage. In the fall, The AeroClinic, will open a second facility in the Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, airport. The staff plans to offer flu shots at mobile kiosks in the airport concourses. For now, travelers must go out of the airport security zone to reach the facility. Stephen Plumlee didn't mind the inconvenience. "I was so out of it, I didn't know what was happening. But everyone has been very helpful." After he rested for a couple of hours and recovered from the nausea, an imbalance in his inner ear was diagnosed. He was given medication to help him cope with the flight home and sent on his way. "This has been good," concluded Plumlee. "It's been fine to be able to do it in the airport, not have to go to some other part of the city and find my way back." E-mail to a friend . Judy Fortin is a correspondent with CNN Medical News.

When the tests revealed no obvious medical problems, Gross received a supply of ibuprofen.

“I took a chance by coming here today, and I’m satisfied,” Gross said. He agreed to follow up with his primary care physician.

“You have 250,000 passengers who come through Atlanta Hartsfield every day, and people are sick,” he said. “What they do is delay their care, or they don’t get their care at all.”

outputs.L2:
ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) — Soon after arriving in Atlanta on a flight from Sarasota, Florida, Stephen Plumlee became nauseated and dizzy. Paramedics took him from the aircraft in a wheelchair, but rather than transporting him to a downtown emergency department, they brought him to a medical clinic in the atrium of the world’s busiest airport.

Known as The AeroClinic, the recently opened walk-in facility provides fast, relatively low-cost treatment for passengers and for some of the airport’s 55,000 workers. It is part of a nationwide rise in conveniently located health centers operating in pharmacies and retail settings.

Dr. Dominic Mack, the clinic’s chief medical officer, described it as a medical stopgap for people who become ill while traveling. In terms of services, The AeroClinic occupies a middle ground between newer, compact retail clinics and the larger, comprehensive after-hours centers that have existed for decades.

For approximately $80, patients with minor, sudden ailments—including headaches, stomach problems and strep throat—can be examined by either a physician or a physician assistant.

Headaches prompted Derrick Gross to seek treatment there. Gross, an Atlanta resident and medical sales representative, is on the road at least three days each week. Because his schedule leaves little time for visits to a regular doctor, he made an appointment after noticing the clinic’s sign while walking through the airport.

Physician assistant Sabrina Jackson spent roughly 20 minutes performing a series of tests in an effort to identify what was causing his headaches. When the results showed no clear medical issue, Gross was provided with ibuprofen. He said he had taken a chance on the clinic and was pleased with the experience. He also agreed to consult his primary care doctor afterward.

According to Mack, many of the clinic’s patients are in situations similar to Gross’. About 250,000 travelers pass through Atlanta Hartsfield each day, he said, and some of them are ill. Often, those passengers postpone medical attention or never receive it.

Frequent traveler and former U.S. Surgeon General Dr. David Satcher said he has personally observed the problem. After traveling nearly 40,000 miles during the previous month, he noted that large numbers of people spend time in airports and that many fail to obtain the care they require.

Satcher, a member of the American Academy of Family Physicians, supports the idea of offering quick medical services inside airports, provided patients remain in contact with their regular physicians at home. He is also an original investor in the privately owned company and sits on The AeroClinic’s board of directors.

At the same time, Satcher emphasized that patients should recognize the clinic’s limitations. It is not an appropriate destination for someone experiencing chest pain, he said. For a minor condition, however, it gives travelers a chance to receive treatment immediately instead of waiting until they return home.

The clinic employs 12 people and also provides preventive services, such as physical examinations, standard immunizations and chronic-disease monitoring. Certain insurance plans are accepted.

A second AeroClinic is scheduled to open in the Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, airport in the fall. Staff members also intend to administer influenza vaccines from mobile kiosks located in airport concourses.

At present, passengers must leave the secure area of the airport to visit the clinic. Plumlee, however, was not bothered by that requirement. He said he had been so disoriented that he did not understand what was going on, but added that everyone had been extremely helpful.

After resting for several hours and recovering from the nausea, Plumlee was diagnosed with an inner-ear imbalance. The clinic gave him medication to make the trip home more manageable and then released him.

Plumlee said the experience had gone well and that receiving treatment at the airport was preferable to traveling elsewhere in Atlanta and then having to find his way back.

Judy Fortin is a correspondent for CNN Medical News.

Atlanta’s AeroClinic offers travelers and airport employees a convenient option for treating minor illnesses without the expense or long wait often associated with a hospital emergency room. Located where busy passengers and workers can reach it easily, the clinic provides quick, affordable care for routine health concerns that require professional attention but are not medical emergencies.

The clinic helps fill a gap between small retail health centers, which may offer only limited services, and full-service emergency departments. Patients can receive basic examinations, testing, and treatment for common illnesses while continuing with their travel or work schedules as quickly as possible. This model is especially useful for people who become sick while away from home, do not have a local doctor, or cannot easily make time for a traditional medical appointment.

Frequent traveler Derrick Gross is one example of a patient who benefited from the service. He was able to obtain convenient testing and basic care without leaving the airport environment or making a lengthy trip to a hospital. For someone managing a demanding travel schedule, that accessibility can make the difference between seeking prompt medical attention and postponing care.

AeroClinic is not intended to replace primary-care physicians or emergency departments. Instead, its staff can address uncomplicated conditions, identify problems that may require more extensive evaluation, and advise patients about appropriate follow-up care. People with serious symptoms can be directed to a hospital, while those who need continued treatment can be referred to a physician or another medical provider.

By placing affordable health services in a high-traffic location, airport clinics such as AeroClinic can expand access to care for people with limited time and few convenient alternatives. They offer a practical way to treat minor health problems early while ensuring that patients are guided toward additional care when necessary.

Atlanta, the capital of Georgia, is one of the most influential cities in the southeastern United States. Known for its rich civil rights history, thriving business community, and major transportation hub, Atlanta also holds an important place in global media.

CNN became the first television channel to provide 24-hour news coverage and transformed how audiences around the world followed breaking events. Its headquarters helped establish Atlanta as a significant center for broadcasting and communications.

Today, Atlanta continues to attract visitors with landmarks such as the Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park, Centennial Olympic Park, and the Georgia Aquarium. The city’s connection to CNN remains an important part of its modern identity and international reputation.
